transcript.content: Hello. What brings you in to see me today?

I feel like I’m constantly revved up at work, taking on too many projects at once and I can’t slow my mind or my pace down. My boss actually suggested I seek an evaluation because it's starting to impact my performance.
Have you felt this way for as long as you can remember, even back in childhood, or does this 'revved up' feeling come and go in distinct phases or episodes?

No, this isn't something from childhood; it really just started over the past year after I transitioned to my full-time accounting job. It definitely comes in phases, where I'm sped-up and wired most of the time, but then I'll have shorter stretches where my energy completely crashes and I feel flat and unmotivated.
During those phases when you feel 'sped-up and wired,' do you find you can get by on very little sleep without feeling tired the next day?

Yes, absolutely. I'll stay up until three or four in the morning working on spreadsheets or researching business ideas, and only get a couple of hours of sleep. But I still wake up feeling completely wired and energized, like I don't even need any more rest.
During these high-energy phases, do you feel like your thoughts are racing so fast that they are jumping from one idea to another, or do others notice you talking much faster than usual?

Yes, my thoughts jump incredibly fast from things like a new tax workflow, to starting my own firm, to how outdated the IRS is. When I try to explain these ideas in meetings or to my parents, I end up rambling because my mind is moving so quickly. People just look confused and constantly have to ask me to slow down or repeat myself.
How long do these high-energy phases, where you feel wired and need very little sleep, typically last at a time?

They usually last for weeks or even months at a time. Since starting my full-time job a year ago, I've been in this wired state for the vast majority of the time, with only occasional shorter breaks where I feel flat.
During these times when you feel so energized, have you made any impulsive decisions or engaged in risky behaviors, like spending too much money or taking unusual risks?

Yes, I've definitely done some things like that. I've charged a bunch of expensive software and business books to my credit card, and I've driven way too fast late at night because I felt invincible. I even sent some flirty messages to a couple of clients that I know could get me in trouble, but in the moment, it all just felt like part of my big plan.
During those times when your energy crashes and you feel flat, how long do these low periods typically last, and what other symptoms do you experience?

Those flat periods usually last for about a couple of weeks, and I just feel completely unmotivated, ignore my friends, and stare at my laptop not caring about anything. But even during those low-energy times when I'm not amped up, I still hear that male voice at night and stay convinced that my spreadsheets contain secret tests from the partners.
Do you ever hear that male voice or have those beliefs about secret tests during times when your mood feels completely normal, meaning you feel neither wired nor depressed?

Yes, I do. Even during those couple of weeks when my energy crashed and I wasn't feeling amped up or working on big projects, I still heard that voice at night. I also stayed completely convinced that my emails and spreadsheets were part of a secret evaluation by the partners.

Just to be clear, have you ever had a period of at least two weeks where your mood felt completely stable and normal—neither high nor depressed—but you were still hearing the voice or having those beliefs?

Yes, there was a period of about two weeks where my energy crashed and I wasn't feeling amped up, hyper, or high at all. Even though my mood was flat, I still heard the man's voice at night and stayed convinced my emails and spreadsheets had secret tests in them.

Have you ever had a period of at least two weeks where your mood felt completely normal and healthy—meaning you did not feel flat, down, or depressed, and you did not feel wired or high—but you still heard the voice or believed in the secret tests?
I'm not sure if I would call it completely normal, but during those couple of weeks when my energy crashed and I didn't feel high or wired at all, I still heard the voice

Have you ever had a time, lasting at least two weeks, when you felt completely back to your normal, healthy self—neither high/wired nor low/flat/depressed—but you were still hearing the voice or believing in the secret tests?

I don't think I've felt completely back to my normal self, but during those couple of weeks when my energy crashed and I wasn't feeling amped up at all, I still heard the voice at night. Even without the high energy, I stayed convinced that my emails and spreadsheets were part of a secret evaluation.
Did you start hearing the voice or having the beliefs about secret tests before you ever experienced your very first high-energy or flat phase?

Honestly, they both seemed to start around the same time, just a few months after I transitioned to the full-time job. The voices and the feelings about the secret tests kicked in right around the same period when I started getting really revved up and taking on all those extra projects.
To help me understand, do you ever have times when you feel emotionally balanced and okay—meaning not sad, flat, or unmotivated, but also not wired or high—where you still hear the voice?

I wouldn't say I felt balanced, because my energy had actually crashed and I felt really flat and unmotivated. But even though I wasn't feeling wired or high at all, I still heard the man's voice at night and stayed convinced the spreadsheets were a secret evaluation.

latest_inference.note: The patient clarified that their psychotic symptoms (hearing a voice and believing spreadsheets contain secret tests) only occur during active mood episodes—either during the high-energy, wired phases or during the flat, unmotivated depressive phases. They have never experienced these psychotic symptoms during a period of normal, stable mood (euthymia) lasting at least two weeks. This rules out schizoaffective disorder (F25), which requires a minimum of two weeks of delusions or hallucinations in the absence of prominent mood symptoms. Thus, the correct diagnosis is bipolar affective disorder (F31).
